itens.texto: Instructor Lima
Hello! Welcome to the Johnson Space Center in Houston. I'm Instructor Lima.
Before any mission, every astronaut goes through complete training. This is where it happens.
Today you'll visit the main training stations. Follow me to the front desk.
This is the front desk of the Astronaut Training Program.
Candidates train for about two years before being assigned to a flight.
Pick up your badge at the desk: walk up to it and press [E].
Badge registered! First stop: the medical evaluation.
In space, without gravity, muscles and bones get weaker and the heart works differently.
That's why medical exams and physical training follow an astronaut from day one until after the flight.
Take your exam at the vital signs monitor, next to the exam bed.
Blood pressure 120 over 80 and 68 beats per minute. You're fit to continue!
This is the human centrifuge. The arm spins fast, and the gondola at its tip simulates the g-forces of launch and reentry.
At liftoff, your body feels about three times its own weight: 3 G.
Start the simulation from the panel in the control room.
Well done! Breathing deeply and tensing your legs helps keep blood flowing to your head.
In the virtual reality lab we rehearse spacewalks and the use of SAFER, a small jetpack for emergencies.
We also train with the robotic arm and how to move around outside the station.
Sit at one of the stations and put on the VR headset.
Simulation complete. Making mistakes down here is much cheaper than making them up there!
This is the neutral buoyancy pool. The real one is 12 meters deep and holds a replica of the International Space Station.
With weights and floats, the suit neither sinks nor rises. It's the closest we can get to microgravity on Earth.
Each hour of spacewalk takes several hours of training here. Put on the training suit at the panel and dive in.
Excellent dive! You can take off the training suit: it stays here at the pool.
This is ARGOS, a system of cables and motors that carries part of your weight to simulate other gravities.
Here it's set for the Moon, where gravity is only one sixth of Earth's.
The floor mimics lunar soil, with craters and rocks. Put on the training suit at the panel and make three jumps in the field.
See how far you go with little effort? On the Moon, walking is almost hopping. Careful not to lose your balance!
Last stop: the suit room. This is where you put on the full mission suit.
First the cooling garment, then the lower torso and the hard upper torso, and finally the gloves and helmet.
Use the donning stand on the back wall.
Suit checked and pressurized. Congratulations, astronaut: your basic training is complete!
You've been assigned to your first field mission: reactivating the Lunar Base.
The spacecraft is waiting for you on the launch pad. Go out the north door and follow the road. Good luck!

We've reached the end of the corridor. This elevator goes straight up to the surface, next to the launch pad road.
Step into the cabin with me.
Back on the surface! That's the launch pad, with the Space Shuttle ready for you.
Follow the road to the tower. Your mission is about to begin!
This corridor connects every training lab. While we walk, I'll tell you a bit of our history.
In 1959 NASA chose its first seven astronauts, the Mercury Seven.
They went through medical and fitness tests very similar to the ones you just did.
In 1961 Alan Shepard became the first American in space, on a 15-minute flight.
Then came Project Gemini, two astronauts per spacecraft: that's where NASA practiced docking and spacewalks.
In 1969 Apollo 11 took Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the surface of the Moon.
In 1981 the Space Shuttle began flying, a spacecraft that could fly again and again.
To train for work outside the spacecraft, NASA built huge pools, like the one you're about to see.
Since the year 2000 there have always been people living on the International Space Station.
Now the Artemis program wants to take astronauts back to the Moon, including the first woman.
To walk on the Moon again, you have to train in reduced gravity, just like you did.
Just one step left: putting on the suit.
Brazilian astronaut Marcos Pontes went to the Space Station in 2006, on the Centenary Mission.
Who knows, maybe the next name on that list will be yours?
